questions.question: A newsvendor's demand $D$ has a continuous, strictly increasing CDF $F(y)=\mathbb{P}(D\le y)$. The critical ratio is $\beta=0.7$, and the optimal stock $y^*$ solves $F(y^*)=0.7$. What does the number 0.7 measure at the stock $y^*$?
options: The expected share of demand served from stock
The expected share of the stocked units that sells
The probability that demand does not exceed stock
The probability that demand exceeds stock

questions.question: In the newsvendor model with selling price $p$, unit cost $c$ and salvage value $s$ (underage cost $b=p-c>0$, overage cost $h=c-s>0$), the critical ratio is $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$. The unit cost $c$ rises while $p$ and $s$ stay fixed. How does $\beta$ change?
options: $\beta$ falls, because $b$ shrinks while $h$ grows.
$\beta$ is unchanged, since the rise in $c$ cancels out.
$\beta$ rises, since dearer units make stockouts costlier.
$\beta$ falls, since its denominator $p-s$ grows.

questions.question: The critical ratio $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$ is defined for underage cost $b=p-c>0$ and overage cost $h=c-s>0$ (price $p$, unit cost $c$, salvage value $s$), so that $0<\beta<1$. A supplier now buys back every unsold unit at its full cost, so $s=c$. What happens to $\beta$?
options: $\beta=0$, so it is best to stock nothing at all.
$\beta$ is undefined, as the formula divides by $h=0$.
$\beta$ is unchanged, as $b=p-c$ does not involve $s$.
$\beta=1$, as unsold units no longer cost anything.

questions.question: A newsvendor has underage cost $b>0$ and overage cost $h>0$ with $b>h$. Demand $D$ has a continuous, strictly increasing CDF $F$, and the optimal stock solves $F(y^*)=\beta$ with $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$. Where does $y^*$ lie?
options: Below the median demand, since $\beta<\frac{1}{2}$
Above the median demand, since $\beta>\frac{1}{2}$
At the mean demand plus $b-h$ extra units
Above every demand level that can occur

questions.question: In the newsvendor model with selling price $p$, unit cost $c$ and salvage value $s$ (underage cost $b=p-c>0$, overage cost $h=c-s>0$), which expression equals the critical ratio $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$?
options: $\frac{p-c}{p}$
$\frac{c-s}{p-s}$
$\frac{p-c}{p-s}$
$\frac{p-c}{c-s}$

questions.question: A shop buys a calendar at $c=6$, sells it at $p=10$, and sells every unsold calendar to a discounter at $s=1$. With underage cost $b=p-c$ and overage cost $h=c-s$, what is the critical ratio $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$?
options: $\frac{4}{9}\approx0.44$
$\frac{5}{9}\approx0.56$

questions.question: A caterer buys a dish at $c=7$ and sells it at $p=12$. Every dish left at the end of the day must be disposed of at a cost of 3 per dish, so the salvage value is $s=-3$. With $b=p-c$ and $h=c-s$, what is the critical ratio $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$?
options: $\frac{5}{12}\approx0.42$
$\frac{5}{9}\approx0.56$
$\frac{2}{3}\approx0.67$
$\frac{1}{3}\approx0.33$

questions.question: A newsvendor's demand has CDF $F(y)=\frac{y-40}{50}$ for $40\le y\le90$ ($F=0$ below 40, $F=1$ above 90). The underage cost is $b=3$ and the overage cost $h=2$, and the optimal stock solves $F(y^*)=\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$. What is $y^*$?

A newsvendor stocks $y_0$ units. Demand has a continuous, strictly increasing CDF $F$ with $F(y_0)=0.6$; the underage cost is $b=5$ and the overage cost $h=3$, and the optimal stock solves $F(y^*)=\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$. How should $y_0$ change?
options: Lower it, as $F(y_0)=0.6$ exceeds $\frac{h}{b+h}=0.375$
Keep it, as $F(y_0)=0.6$ already exceeds one half
Raise it, as $F(y_0)=0.6$ is below $\frac{b}{b+h}=0.625$
Lower it, as the stockout chance $0.4$ is below $0.625$

questions.question: A retailer buys an item at $c=4$ and can sell each unsold unit for $s=1$. For which selling price $p$ is the critical ratio $\beta=\frac{p-c}{p-s}$ equal to $0.75$?

A newsvendor has stocked $y$ units and considers one more. Demand has CDF $F(y)=\mathbb{P}(D\le y)$; the extra unit is left over (loss $h>0$) when $D\le y$ and is sold (avoiding a lost margin $b>0$) when $D>y$. When does the extra unit lower the expected cost?
options: When $F(y)<\frac{b}{b+h}$
When $F(y)<\frac{h}{b+h}$
When $F(y)>\frac{b}{b+h}$
When $F(y)<\frac{b}{h}$

questions.question: In the newsvendor model with selling price $p$, unit cost $c$ and salvage value $s$ (underage cost $b=p-c>0$, overage cost $h=c-s>0$), which change leaves the critical ratio $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$ unchanged for every amount $k>0$?
options: A price rise and an equal unit-cost rise, salvage fixed
Equal rises in the price, unit cost and salvage value
A cost rise matched by a salvage rise, price fixed
A higher price and an equally higher salvage value

questions.question: For a newsvendor with underage cost $b>0$ and overage cost $h>0$, the critical ratio is $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$. The underage cost doubles to $2b$ while $h$ stays fixed. How does the critical ratio change?
options: It doubles, because $\beta$ is proportional to $b$.
It stays the same, because $b$ appears above and below.
The stockout probability $1-\beta$ is cut exactly in half.
It rises less than twofold, as its odds $\frac{b}{h}$ double.

questions.question: A shop's daily demand is 100 units on nine days out of ten and 300 units on the tenth. It stocks 100 units each day, so demand does not exceed stock with probability 0.9, its critical ratio. Over ten such days, what share of total demand is served from stock?
options: About 93%
Exactly 90%
About 83%
Exactly 100%

questions.question: A newsvendor sells at $p=10$, buys at $c=6$, and demand has CDF $F(y)=\frac{y-100}{100}$ for $100\le y\le200$. Unsold units were worthless ($s=0$); a buy-back deal now pays $s=2$ per unsold unit. The optimal stock solves $F(y^*)=\beta=\frac{p-c}{p-s}$. How does $y^*$ change?
options: It rises by 10 units
It does not change
It falls by 10 units
It rises by 20 units

questions.question: Daily demand takes the values 20, 21, 22, 23, 24 with probabilities 0.1, 0.25, 0.3, 0.2, 0.15. The underage cost is $b=7$ and the overage cost $h=3$, and raising stock from $y$ to $y+1$ lowers expected cost exactly when $\mathbb{P}(D\le y)<\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$. Which stock is best?

For a newsvendor with price $p$, unit cost $c$ and salvage value $s$, where $p>c>s\ge0$, a buyer uses the gross margin ratio $m=\frac{p-c}{p}$ in place of the critical ratio $\beta=\frac{p-c}{p-s}$. How do $m$ and $\beta$ compare?
options: $\beta$ is below $m$ whenever salvage is positive
$\beta$ equals $m$ for every salvage value used
Either can be larger, depending on $p$ and $c$
$\beta$ exceeds $m$ whenever salvage is positive

questions.question: Two newsvendor products have critical ratios $\beta_A=0.9$ and $\beta_B=0.3$, where $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$ with underage cost $b$ and overage cost $h$. Their demand distributions are unknown. Which conclusion follows from these ratios alone?
options: A is stocked at a higher quantile of its own demand.
A earns a larger margin on every unit that it sells.
A should be stocked in more units than product B.
A loses less money on each unsold unit than B does.

questions.question: An item has overage cost $h=6$ per leftover unit. Its manager insists on stocking so that demand does not exceed stock with probability 0.95, and the optimal stock is the one where this probability equals the critical ratio $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$. For which underage cost $b$ (lost margin per unit short) would this policy be optimal?

Daily demand is 10, 11, 12 or 13 with probabilities 0.2, 0.4, 0.3, 0.1. With underage cost $b=3$, overage cost $h=2$ and critical ratio $\beta=\frac{b}{b+h}$, raising stock from $y$ to $y+1$ changes expected cost by $h\,\mathbb{P}(D\le y)-b\,\mathbb{P}(D>y)$. Which whole-number stocks give the smallest expected cost?
options: Only 11, the first stock with $\mathbb{P}(D\le y)\ge\beta$
Both 11 and 12, as $\mathbb{P}(D\le 11)=\beta$ holds exactly
Only 12, the first stock with $\mathbb{P}(D\le y)>\beta$
Only 10, the last stock with $\mathbb{P}(D\le y)<\beta$
